summary: Describes an experimental change to RFC 3168 that adds Explicit Congestion Notification capability to TCP SYN/ACK packets. It does not claim consensus that this is the best use of ECN, though it can be deployed in the current Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5562 lets a TCP server mark its reply to a connection request as willing to be told about congestion. A busy router can then flag that reply instead of discarding it, and the server replies again without the flag and starts sending data more slowly. The connection avoids a three second wait.

subtitle: Letting the reply to a connection request be marked as congested instead of thrown away, so a new connection does not wait three seconds.

tldr.problem: When a router is congested it drops packets, and a TCP connection whose opening reply is dropped has to wait for a three second retransmission timeout before it can start.
tldr.mechanism: The memo allows the reply to a connection request to be marked as ECN-Capable, so a congested router marks it instead of dropping it. The sender then reduces its initial congestion window to one segment and repeats the reply without the ECN-Capable mark.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. The memo says the proposal may be deployed in the current Internet but does not represent a consensus that this is the best mechanism for using ECN in those packets.

today: RFC 5562 is an Experimental document from June 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo states that the proposal is Experimental, that it may be deployed in the current Internet, and that it does not represent a consensus that this is the best possible mechanism for the use of ECN in TCP SYN/ACK packets. It asks for measurement studies of routers and middleboxes before widespread deployment.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TCP's congestion control has primarily used packet loss as the congestion indication, with packets dropped when buffers overflow. With such tail-drop mechanisms the packet delay can be high, since the queue at bottleneck routers can be fairly large, and dropping packets only when the queue overflows and having TCP react only to such losses results in significantly higher packet delay, unnecessarily many packet losses, and unfairness due to synchronization effects. The adoption of active queue management allows better control of bottleneck queues, giving better control of the queue with reduced queuing delay, fewer packet drops, and better fairness because of fewer synchronization effects.

With the adoption of ECN, performance may be further improved. When the router detects congestion before buffer overflow it can either drop a packet or set the Congestion Experienced codepoint in the ECN field of the IP header. For incremental deployment and backwards compatibility, routers may mark ECN-Capable packets that would otherwise have been dropped. Using ECN lets TCP react to congestion while avoiding unnecessary retransmission timeouts. This benefits short transfers, where a connection's congestion window may hold only one packet and a drop forces a wait for a retransmission timeout, and longer flows, which may see less loss and avoid retransmissions.

RFC 3168 specifies setting the ECN-Capable codepoint on TCP data packets, but not on TCP SYN and SYN/ACK packets, and specifies the negotiation of ECN between the two TCP endpoints in the SYN and SYN-ACK exchange using flags in the TCP header. Erring on the side of being conservative, it does not specify the use of ECN for the first SYN/ACK packet itself. This memo specifies that use, because of the high cost of a dropped SYN/ACK packet and the resulting retransmission timeout, and because the connection has not yet started placing a load on the network. The stated benefits are the avoidance of a retransmission timeout and an improvement in the throughput of short connections.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is the delay at the very start of a connection. The reply from the server can be lost in a busy router, and then the client waits three seconds before trying again. Marking that reply instead of dropping it tells the server to be more careful, without costing the client any delay.

sections.title: Conventions and Terminology
sections.content:
The memo uses the terminology of RFC 3168. In the IP header, the ECN field carries the CE codepoint, the Congestion Experienced one, and ECT, either one of the two ECN-Capable Transport codepoints. In the TCP header, the ECN flags are CWR, the Congestion Window Reduced flag, and ECE, the ECN-Echo flag. An ECN-setup SYN packet is a SYN packet with the ECE and CWR flags, and an ECN-setup SYN-ACK packet is a SYN-ACK packet with ECE but not CWR. The memo calls the sender of the SYN packet the initiator and the sender of the SYN/ACK packet the responder.

The point of the ECT codepoint is that it marks a packet as able to react to a congestion signal, so a router may mark it rather than drop it. The ECE flag in the TCP header is how the receiver passes that signal back to the sender, and CWR is how the sender acknowledges that it has reacted.
sections.plainLanguage: Three labels matter. ECT in the IP header says the packet can be told about congestion instead of being dropped. ECE in the TCP header is how that news is passed back to the sender. CWR is how the sender says it has acted on it.

sections.title: The Specification
sections.content:
Section 6.1.1 of RFC 3168 states that a host MUST NOT set ECT on SYN or SYN/ACK packets. This memo specifies that a TCP node may respond to an initial ECN-setup SYN packet by setting ECT in the responding ECN-setup SYN/ACK packet, indicating to routers that the SYN/ACK packet is ECN-Capable. This allows a congested router along the path to mark the packet instead of dropping it as an indication of congestion.

The mechanism is called ECN+/TryOnce, and it differs from the original proposal for ECN+. Assume that node A transmits to node B an ECN-setup SYN packet indicating willingness to use ECN, and that node B is willing, so it responds with an ECN-setup SYN/ACK packet.

If the SYN/ACK packet is dropped in the network, the responder waits three seconds for the retransmission timer to expire and then retransmits the SYN/ACK packet. If a SYN/ACK packet with the ECT codepoint is dropped, the responder should resend the SYN/ACK packet without the ECN-Capable codepoint. The memo notes that if syn-cookies were used by the responder, it would not set a timer on sending the SYN/ACK, and the initiator would have to time out and retransmit the SYN packet instead.

If the SYN/ACK packet is ECN-marked in the network instead of dropped, the initiator restarts the retransmission timer, sets the ECN-Echo flag in the TCP header of the responding ACK packet, and uses the standard rules for the cumulative acknowledgement field. The initiator does not advance from the SYN-Sent to the Established state until it receives a SYN/ACK packet that is not ECN-marked. When the responder receives the ECN-Echo packet reporting the Congestion Experienced indication, it sets the initial congestion window to one segment instead of the two allowed by RFC 2581 or the three or four allowed by RFC 3390, and sends a SYN/ACK packet that is not ECN-Capable. The responder does not advance the send sequence number and it sets the retransmission timer, following RFC 2988 for the value. The TCP hosts follow the standard rules for duplicate SYN/ACK packets.

The mechanism differs from RFC 3168 in two respects. RFC 3168 does not allow SYN/ACK packets to be ECN-Capable, and it says the sending TCP MUST restart the retransmission timer on receiving the ECN-Echo packet when the congestion window is one. RFC 3168 also has the TCP responder set the CWR flag in the next data packet to acknowledge its receipt of the ECN-Echo flag, whereas in this memo the responder does not set CWR but simply sends a SYN/ACK packet that is not ECN-Capable, after which the initiator clears the ECN-Echo flag on its replying packets. If the second SYN/ACK is also dropped, the responder's timer expires and it resends the SYN/ACK, following the TCP standards.

The memo also asks that a TCP implementation using ECN-Capable SYN/ACK packets include a management interface to allow the use of ECN to be turned off for those packets, to deal with possible backwards compatibility problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Here is the whole exchange. The server sends its reply marked as markable. If a router marks it instead of dropping it, the client passes the news back in the acknowledgement and waits for a second, unmarked reply. The server sends that second reply, shrinks its starting window to one segment, and only then does the client start sending data.

sections.title: Why SYN/ACK Packets Are Treated Differently
sections.content:
The memo gives the rationale. When node B receives a TCP SYN packet with the ECN-Echo bit set, this indicates that node A is ECN-Capable, and if node B is also ECN-Capable there are no obstacles to immediately setting one of the ECN-Capable codepoints in the IP header of the responding SYN/ACK packet. Congestion is most likely to occur in the server-to-client direction, so marking the SYN/ACK can reduce the occurrence of three-second retransmission timeouts.

Two security arguments are made against setting the ECN-Capable codepoint in the initiating SYN packet. First, when the SYN packet is sent there are no guarantees that the other endpoint is ECN-Capable, or that it would understand and react if the CE codepoint was set by a congested router. Second, the codepoint in SYN packets could be misused by malicious clients to improve the well-known TCP SYN attack, by injecting a large number of SYN packets through a potentially congested ECN-enabled router and congesting it further. For both reasons the restriction that the SYN packet must not have the ECN-Capable codepoint set is continued.

The memo also examines the size question. There are router buffer architectures that have smaller dropping rates for small packets than for large ones. For a Drop-Tail queue in units of packets, small and large packets are equally likely to be dropped, while for a Drop-Tail queue in units of bytes, small packets are less likely to be dropped. Similarly, for RED in packet mode small and large packets are equally likely to be dropped or marked, while for RED in byte mode a packet's chance is proportional to its size in bytes. So for a congested router with an AQM in byte mode the drop rate for SYN/ACK packets should generally be low and the benefit of making them ECN-Capable should be similarly moderate, whereas for a router with a packet-based queue and no priority queuing the benefit should be significant.

On the response to a marked SYN/ACK, the memo argues that ECN gives end systems a wider range of possible responses than waiting a default time. It notes that halving the congestion window is not the same as halving the sending rate, since there is no sending rate associated with an ECN-Capable SYN/ACK packet, and that a router's marking of a SYN/ACK packet is not affected by any past history of the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client must not mark its opening request, for two reasons: the server may not understand the mark, and a malicious client could use it to flood a busy router. The server's reply is a different matter, because the server already knows the client understands the mark.

sections.title: Performance Evaluation
sections.content:
The memo compares three possible responses by a TCP node to a report of an ECN-marked SYN/ACK packet. With ECN+, the original proposal, the node sets the initial congestion window to one segment and immediately sends a data packet, if it has one to send. With ECN+/Wait, the node sets the initial congestion window to one segment and waits a round-trip time before sending a data packet, since the responder already has one measurement of the round-trip time when the acknowledgement arrives. With ECN+/TryOnce, the mechanism specified in this memo, the responder replies to a report of an ECN-marked SYN/ACK packet by sending a SYN/ACK packet that is not ECN-Capable and reducing the initial congestion window to one segment.

Simulations comparing Standard ECN without ECN-marked SYN/ACK packets, ECN+, ECN+/Wait and ECN+/TryOnce show little difference between ECN+ and ECN+/Wait in terms of aggregate congestion. However, for some scenarios with queues that are packet-based rather than byte-based, and with packet drop rates above 25% without ECN+, the use of ECN+ or of ECN+/Wait can more than double the packet drop rates to greater than 50%. ECN+/TryOnce does not increase the packet drop rate in scenarios of high congestion, while giving a performance improvement similar to that of the other two. The memo concludes that ECN+/TryOnce is safe, has significant benefits to the user, and avoids the problems of ECN+ and ECN+/Wait under extreme congestion. It notes that the congestion-related problems of ECN+ and ECN+/Wait were only discovered when the simulations were re-run with an updated version of the ns-2 simulator, after the document had almost completed the standardization process.

The memo also notes that the percentage of SYN/ACK packets on a link can be quite high: measurements on links dominated by web traffic indicate that 15 to 20% of the packets can be SYN/ACK packets. The drop of a SYN/ACK packet can increase the download time of a short file by an order of magnitude, by requiring a three-second retransmission timeout, while for longer-lived flows the effect is less dramatic, though the change can still improve fairness among long-lived flows because newly arriving flows are less likely to have to wait for retransmission timeouts.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo tried three ways of reacting to a marked reply. The one it settles on is the only one that does not make a bad network worse: the other two could double the packet loss rate in the worst tests.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
TCP packets carrying the ECT codepoint in IP headers can be marked rather than dropped by ECN-Capable routers, which raises security concerns.

The first known deployment problem, dating back to 2000, is a small but decreasing number of routers or middleboxes that reset a TCP connection in response to TCP SYN packets using flags in the TCP header to negotiate ECN-Capability. Another problem reported in 2007 concerns routers that crash when a TCP data packet arrives with the ECN field set to ECT(0) or ECT(1). While there is no evidence that any routers or middleboxes drop SYN/ACK packets that contain an ECN-Capable or CE codepoint in the IP header, such behavior cannot be excluded, and there seem to be a number of routers or middleboxes that drop TCP SYN packets containing known or unknown IP options. That is why the specification says that if a SYN/ACK packet with the ECT or CE codepoint is dropped, the TCP node should resend it without the ECN-Capable codepoint.

On congestion collapse, the concern is whether marking SYN/ACK packets instead of dropping them could invoke congestion or worsen performance in highly congested scenarios. After learning that a SYN/ACK packet was ECN-marked, the responder sends one that is not ECN-Capable, and if that one is dropped the responder waits for a retransmission timeout as the TCP standards require. Routers are also free to drop rather than mark arriving packets when congestion is very high, and when a router's buffer is full it has no choice but to drop.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old routers and middleboxes misbehave when they see ECN bits. The memo cannot rule out that one might drop a marked reply, which is why the reply is always repeated without the mark if that happens. The concern that marking would make a congested network worse is answered by the simulations and by the fact that the second reply is not markable.

viz.caption: THE CODIPOINTS AND FLAGS THIS CHANGE RELIES ON

items.label: ECN-Capable Transport
items.desc: One of two codepoints in the ECN field of the IP header, set by a sender willing to react to a congestion mark.

items.label: Congestion Experienced
items.desc: Set in the ECN field of the IP header by a router that is congested.

items.label: ECN-Echo
items.desc: A TCP header flag used to report a congestion mark back to the sender.

items.label: Congestion Window Reduced
items.desc: A TCP header flag used to acknowledge receipt of the ECN-Echo flag.

viz.caption: THE ECN+/TRYONCE EXCHANGE WHEN THE REPLY IS MARKED

messages.label: ECN-SETUP SYN
messages.note: The client offers to use ECN.

messages.label: SYN/ACK, ECT
messages.note: The server marks its reply as ECN-Capable and sets a timer.

messages.label: SYN/ACK, CE
messages.note: The congested router marks the reply instead of dropping it.

messages.label: ACK, ECN-ECHO
messages.note: The client passes the mark back and does not yet enter the Established state.

messages.label: SYN/ACK, not ECT
messages.note: The server repeats the reply without the mark and sets its initial window to one segment.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS OF REACTING TO A MARKED SYN/ACK

Sets the initial congestion window to one segment and waits a round-trip time before sending a data packet.
Sets the initial congestion window to one segment and sends a SYN/ACK packet that is not ECN-Capable. This is the mechanism the memo specifies.
